correctness.rationale: For a finite invariant support, each deterministic map permutes that support. On two points the only possibilities are the identity and the transposition. If \(T_\beta\) transposes \(x,y\), then \((\beta+1)(x-y)\) is a nonzero integer. If \(T_\gamma\) also transposes, then \((\gamma+1)/(\beta+1)\) is rational; substituting \(\gamma+1=(m/n)\beta+2-m/n\) and comparing coefficients of the irrational number \(\beta\) forces \(m=n\), contrary to \(\gamma\ne\beta\). If one map transposes and the other fixes the support pointwise, the same integer-difference argument forces either \((\gamma-1)/(\beta+1)\) or \((\gamma+1)/(\beta-1)\) to be rational, and coefficient comparison gives a contradiction. Hence both maps fix both atoms. A point \(z\in[0,1)\) is fixed by \(T_b\) exactly when \((b-1)z\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\); with \(\gamma-1=(m/n)(\beta-1)\) in lowest terms this gives exactly \(z=n\ell/(\beta-1)\) with \(n\ell<\beta-1\). Thus every common invariant measure with support at most two is supported on the stated common fixed-point set.
residual_risks: The theorem is confined to support cardinality at most two on the excluded rational-affine relation.
No claim is made about three-point cycles or nonatomic singular common invariant measures.
